statement: The system shall help people quickly find the right information or service at the point of need.
The system shall not require staff intervention.
The kiosk shall be easy to understand.
The kiosk shall be forgiving.
The kiosk shall let users continue what they were doing even if they switch from touch to voice or encounter a problem.
Operational reliability shall have the highest priority in trade-offs.
The system shall remain usable in a public setting and shall not leave users stranded.
The kiosk shall provide clear guidance and low effort for occasional users.
Adaptability shall be the lowest priority among the stated trade-off priorities.
The kiosk's adaptability shall not make the experience unpredictable or harder to trust.
The system shall provide public visitors with a very simple, guided experience that works even if they are unfamiliar with the kiosk.
Staff nearby shall be able to assist users.
Administrators and support teams shall have stable system operation.
Administrators and support teams shall be able to recover from errors quickly.
Content owners shall be able to keep the information current and context-sensitive.
If partner service providers are connected to the access point, the system shall provide a reliable integration point.
If partner service providers are connected to the access point, the system shall enforce clear rules for what data or services can be exposed.
The kiosk shall prefer content that matches the user's current context first, rather than showing a generic menu.
The kiosk shall consider the user's current context to include location, current task, and the interaction the user was already in.
If multiple options fit, the kiosk shall present the most relevant and simplest path first.
The kiosk shall show content restricted by eligibility or access rights only if the user qualifies or explicitly identifies themselves.
If the needed content or service is unavailable, the kiosk shall not fail silently.
If the needed content or service is unavailable, the kiosk shall offer the closest alternative when one is available.
If the backend is down or uncertain, the kiosk shall show a safe fallback rather than guess.
The Accesspoint shall support public users in a practical way.
The Accesspoint shall provide clear guidance.
The Accesspoint shall maintain stable behavior across different interaction modes.
The interviewee will call out assumptions that seem off once details are discussed.
The Accesspoint shall remain understandable when the network is slow.
The Accesspoint shall remain understandable when the network is temporarily unavailable.
The project is starting from scratch or replacing a very basic setup.
The system shall allow a user to switch interaction modes without having to repeat themselves.
The system shall support a user reading options on screen and then asking a question out loud as part of the same interaction.
The transition between visual and spoken interaction shall feel natural.
The system shall work for people with different abilities.
The system shall provide full spoken guidance.
The system shall be forgiving when the user makes a mistake and allow the user to back up without losing progress.
The system shall confirm important choices before committing them.
When the network is slow or unavailable, the system shall clearly tell the user what is happening.
The system shall remember what the user has already done during the current session.
The system shall remember the user's selected language during the current session.
The system should avoid storing anything too personal beyond the session unless there is a clear need and approval for it.
The system shall involve the people who operate and support the kiosks in requirements consideration.
The system shall account for the real-world failures that kiosk operators and support staff know about.
The system shall involve public users in requirements consideration.
The system shall involve the owners of connected services in requirements consideration.
The system shall depend on the data provided by connected services.
People shall be able to walk up to the Accesspoint and complete common tasks without help.
The kiosks shall be manageable to maintain.
The service owners shall trust the Accesspoint to present correct, up-to-date information.
The system shall make content and services easy to update as public information changes.
The system shall make it obvious to users when they are using public, shared equipment.
The system shall help users understand that their session on public, shared equipment is temporary.
The system shall provide people with a simple way to get the right information or service when they need it.
The system shall help people find context-sensitive information.
The system shall help people complete common public-service tasks.
The system shall especially support occasional users who are not familiar with the system and need guidance to finish what they came for.
The access point shall be intended for public terminals and kiosks in places where people need quick access to services.
The access point should not be used in settings where the user needs a private or highly secure workstation experience unless stronger controls are added.
The terminal shall have a decent-sized screen that is easy to read at standing distance.
The terminal shall support touch input.
The terminal may include a card reader and printer depending on the service, but they are optional add-ons rather than universal requirements.
The terminal camera requirement shall depend on whether the system needs identity verification, video assistance, or an accessibility feature that uses a camera.
The system shall use simple, service-oriented wording for user-facing actions.
The system shall use more operational wording for staff-facing language.
The system shall avoid jargon and internal department terms unless the user is already in that context.
The access point shall connect to back-end service platforms that hold the actual information and requests.
The access point shall connect to authentication or identity services to support session resumption and user verification.
The access point shall connect to content or knowledge systems to retrieve context-sensitive information for the location and task.
The connections shall enable users to search.
The connections shall enable users to continue transactions without restarting when they switch interaction modes or when the terminal temporarily loses connectivity.
The system shall display information that helps the user complete the task they came for.
If the user has already started something, the system shall display the progress or saved session so the user can pick up where they left off.
The system shall display sensitive information only after the appropriate level of verification.
The system shall support exceptions for sites with stronger privacy needs.
The system shall support exceptions for sites with stronger accessibility needs.
A public terminal in a secure area shall use tighter session handling.
A public terminal in a very busy lobby shall provide simpler flows.
The system may exclude printing as a function at some sites.
The system may exclude access to sensitive records as a function at some sites.
In a secure area, the session should time out fairly quickly if the terminal is idle.
If the user steps away or there is a significant pause, the user should re-authenticate before continuing.
The system should require re-authentication after certain mode changes when the new mode exposes more personal or transactional information.
The system should block viewing protected records until the user is verified again.
If the network drops, the terminal shall keep the user informed.
If the network drops, the terminal shall preserve what it can locally.
The terminal shall present fewer choices on each screen and place only the most common actions up front.
The terminal shall use stronger prompts and clear next-step guidance so users do not have to think too much or wander through menus.
The terminal shall confirm selections quickly and avoid long explanatory text unless the user asks for help.
If there are multiple ways to complete something, the terminal shall nudge users toward the fastest path first.
For sensitive services, the terminal should not show contextual information that might reveal information before the user is verified.
The system should work on standard kiosk hardware with a display.
The system should provide audio only when a headset or speakers are actually present.
The system should support operation in poor connectivity.
The system should allow users to still get guidance in degraded mode.
The system should not hardcode a specific screen size unless a site has a special kiosk format.
Screen-size requirements should be deployment-specific when a site has a special kiosk format.
For the initial rollout, the terminal should be placed in locations where people already need quick, guided access to common services.
Initial rollout locations should include reception areas, service counters, and public lobbies.
Initial rollout sites should have relatively stable staffing and network support.
Initial rollout sites should allow testing of secure-session behavior and degraded-network handling without too much operational risk.
The system shall customize local hours for the new location.
The system shall customize directions for the new location.
The system shall customize forms for the new location.
The system shall customize service names for the new location.
The system shall retire outdated or site-specific legacy content instead of copying it forward.
The system shall keep shared interaction patterns consistent across terminals.
The system shall adapt services that depend on local rules during deployment.
If audio is not reliable, the terminal shall fall back cleanly to a fully visual and touch-based flow without making the user repeat anything.
The task shall remain achievable end to end when voice is not available.
The system shall detect unreliable audio early and present the simpler interaction mode by default for that site.
The terminal shall adapt to the kiosk it is installed on rather than rely on one fixed screen size.
The deployment shall define a supported screen class and orientation for each site.
If a location uses a narrow portrait kiosk or a wider landscape kiosk, the layouts and touch targets shall be tuned accordingly.
The visual fallback shall remain usable on kiosks with different screen shapes and sizes.
Sites where the visual fallback is the main experience shall use simpler screens.
Sites where the visual fallback is the main experience shall use larger controls by default.
The system shall accommodate users with varying skill levels.
The system shall not slow down repeat users.
The system shall account for users with accessibility needs.
The terminal shall support simple, high-frequency public-service tasks that people can complete in a few guided steps.
The terminal shall support finding local services.
The terminal shall support getting directions.
The terminal shall support starting an application.
The terminal shall not support complex case handling or tasks requiring a lot of specialist staff intervention.
The terminal shall only offer tasks that the site can actually support.
If a task cannot be completed on-screen, the terminal shall either save the progress and hand the user off to staff or clearly explain the next step.
The terminal shall not let the user reach a dead end when a task cannot be completed on-screen.
The terminal shall hand the user off to staff immediately when the request is too complex, sensitive, or clearly outside the terminal’s scope.
The system shall move the user to the right person or counter as smoothly as possible in those cases.
The terminal shall always make available basic orientation and wayfinding tasks.
These basic orientation and wayfinding tasks shall be available at any site and shall not depend heavily on local back-end systems.
The terminal shall only display more specific tasks when the site actually supports them and when the hours or conditions allow staff or the system to handle follow-through.
The terminal shall hide or adjust some simple tasks based on local operating conditions rather than showing them everywhere all the time.

The system shall determine task availability based on whether the site is open for the service, whether the relevant department or backend is available, and whether local staff handoff is possible at that time.
If availability conditions change while a user is in the middle of a task, the terminal shall preserve the user's progress and clearly explain that the service is no longer available.
The kiosk shall detect missing required fields.
The kiosk shall detect invalid formats.
The kiosk shall detect out-of-range values.
The kiosk shall detect entries that do not match the expected selection.
For ambiguous or unreadable inputs, the kiosk shall tell the user what it thought they entered and allow the user to retry or choose again.
For fixed public kiosks, touch shall be the primary input method.
For fixed public kiosks, keyboard support or mouse support may be optional depending on the installation.
In staffed or semi-public terminal setups, keyboard and mouse should be available more often because the environment is more controlled.
If a task depends on missing hardware, the terminal shall explain this clearly and offer the nearest supported alternative.
The system shall determine the default active input method based on the installation context and the last mode the user was actively using in that session, provided that this still makes sense.
In a noisy public area, touch input should remain the primary input method.
If the user starts with speech input, the system shall continue to favor speech input until the user switches away from it.
Users shall be able to switch input modes explicitly at any time through a clear on-screen control or a voice command.
The system shall keep the previous mode as the default only if the environment still supports it and the user has not indicated a preference for something else.
If the environment changes in a way that makes the previous mode impractical, the system shall switch automatically to the most reliable available mode.
If the available modes differ by location, the local installation shall take precedence over the remembered preference.
Site conditions should affect the supported screen class and orientation for a kiosk.
The chosen orientation must keep the interface readable and operable without forcing users into awkward gestures or hidden controls.
The terminal shall prioritize keeping the user's task understandable and recoverable.
The terminal shall avoid crashing.
The terminal shall limit tasks that require a lot of back-and-forth to starting the process, collecting the basic details, or directing the user to the right staff or service desk.
The terminal shall explain what it can do in cases where it can only support a task in a limited way.
The system shall interrupt the current flow only for serious cases.
The system shall vary how forceful and immediate an interruption message is based on the urgency level.
For safety or privacy issues, the interruption message wording shall be direct and unmistakable.
For safety or privacy issues, the spoken announcement shall be brief but strong enough to get attention right away.
For less urgent interruptions, the message wording shall be calmer and more explanatory.
For less urgent interruptions where the user only needs to retry or wait for service to return, the message shall be calmer and more explanatory.
If staff is already nearby, the terminal may be less repetitive.
The public kiosk shall send more than the minimum necessary data only when it is needed to complete the user's chosen task or to recover from a failure.
If a service genuinely needs a location, reference number, or session context to continue, the public kiosk may send that information.
The system shall proceed only if the user is clearly present.
The system shall proceed only if the session is still active.
For sensitive data, the system shall require reauthentication or a simple confirmation before display.
The system shall recheck when there is any sign of role mismatch.
The system shall recheck when there is a timeout.
The system shall recheck when there is an interrupted handoff to staff.
The system shall keep the core meaning consistent across all modes.
The system shall allow the presentation to vary across modes.
The spoken version shall be more conversational.
Consistency should take priority over perfectly tailoring every mode.
The core action should remain clearly recognizable as the same thing on screen.
The system shall show required details in partial form where possible.
The system shall allow a reference number or confirmation code to be shown when it is necessary to complete the task.
The system shall allow a name or location to be shown in limited form when it is needed to confirm the correct record.
Partial details are acceptable only when the context is safe enough for a public display.
The system shall update continuously in the background as new service data arrives.
The system shall perform background updates without interrupting the user.
The system shall increase update frequency when the terminal displays time-sensitive information such as queue status or availability.
The system shall decrease update frequency when the user is in the middle of a form or guided flow.
The system shall slow updates and avoid constant refreshing when the network is unstable or the content is low urgency.
The system shall ensure updates do not make the current task feel jumpy or unsafe.
If the user is entering data, reading a multi-step explanation, or in the middle of a sensitive action, the system shall slow down updates a lot or pause them until that step is done.
If the screen is just showing status, wait times, or other live information, the system may refresh more often as long as it does not interrupt the flow.
When the network is unstable, the system shall back off automatically and shall not retry so aggressively that it becomes distracting.
The system shall resume normal refreshing once the connection is stable again.
For some specialist cases, the system shall go beyond a simple handoff and prepare the case properly before transferring it.
The system shall collect the essential context when it can do so.
The system shall summarize the issue when it can do so.
The system shall route the user to the right live agent or service when it can do so.
The system shall not simply point the user away immediately when it can prepare the case properly before transferring it.
If the terminal cannot safely support the workflow or the user needs something that must be handled in person, the system shall stop sooner and direct the user to the right place.
The system shall only proceed when it can add real value without risking a bad or incomplete transfer.
The system shall support public-facing terminals and kiosks for users who need quick access to services and information with minimal training.
The system shall support users switching between touch input, voice input, and other input modes.
The system shall handle interruptions caused by mistakes, weak connectivity, and changes in context.
The system shall make public services and information more accessible in places where staff assistance is limited.
The system shall provide a modern access experience.
The project shall improve service and create efficiency opportunities.
The system shall treat task completion rate as an important success metric.
The system shall capture user satisfaction through short post-use feedback if possible.
Exact target numbers for these measures shall be agreed with the business and operations teams.
The main stakeholders are the end users at the kiosks.
Service owners and operations staff define what information and transactions the Accesspoint system should expose.
Service owners shall define the user needs to be accomplished and identify the content or transactions that are most important.
Conflicts shall be balanced between user needs and what is maintainable.

Operations staff care about what happens when something goes wrong in the field.

Project-specific jargon should be confirmed with the team before being assumed.

The system shall choose a fallback or recovery action based on the type of failure and how far the user has progressed in the task.
The system shall support users with different abilities or levels of confidence with technology.
The user should always know what happened and what to do next.
The system should decide when to offer help proactively versus when to stay out of the way so it does not overwhelm people.
The system shall be easy to approach.

Operations shall address supportability in the field.
Service owners shall decide what best fits the business need.
Those groups shall review changes together before anything is finalized.
The system shall make fallback behavior feel supportive rather than punishing.

The system shall determine when help is offered based on whether a user seems stuck.
The system shall leave experienced users alone when offering help.
